findings.title: No code computes the AUROC results (Fig. 5, §4.3, Fig. 9-11)
findings.claim: Section 4.3 / Appendix D.3 report AUROC for confidence and entropy estimations (e.g. 80.45 / 82.19), and D.3 says AUROC is 'implemented by sklearn toolkit', but no file in code/ imports sklearn or computes roc_auc / AUROC (grep over code/*.py returns zero matches).
findings.concern: An entire reported analysis (reliability of the uncertainty estimations) has no producing script in the repo, so those numbers cannot be reproduced or checked.
findings.resolution: Authors: please add the AUROC computation script (the code that reads confidence/entropy predictions vs correctness labels and calls sklearn's roc_auc_score) used for Fig. 5 and Fig. 9-11.
findings.reason: Repo-wide grep for auroc/auc/roc_auc/sklearn/roc_curve over code/*.py returns zero matches, confirming no AUROC computation exists; paper_text.txt:975-990 and :2049-2058 confirm the 80.45/82.19 AUROC numbers and the sklearn-toolkit claim.

findings.title: Reward model (Eq. 6) is never trained; Table 2 accuracy has no code
findings.claim: uncertainty.py::reward_dataset() builds and (line 159) writes a reward-training file, but no script reads the '*_reward' directory and no code trains a binary reward classifier (no AutoModelForSequenceClassification / num_labels / BCE anywhere). train_ppo.py instead loads the reward as a plain AutoModelForCausalLM. Table 2 (reward-model accuracy) therefore has no producing/evaluating code.
findings.concern: The reward model is a central component (Eq. 6, Algorithm 1 stage 1, Table 2) but its training and accuracy evaluation are absent, so Table 2 cannot be reproduced and the PPO reward signal has no defined source.
findings.resolution: Authors: please add the reward-model SFT/classifier training script and the script that computes the Table 2 reward-model accuracy.
findings.reason: uncertainty.py:152-156 quote matches verbatim; no train_*.py references "_reward" (only uncertainty.py:129 builds the path for writing) and repo-wide grep for SequenceClassification/num_labels/BCE finds nothing; train_ppo.py:233 confirms reward_model is loaded via AutoModelForCausalLM.

findings.title: train_ppo.py does not compile (duplicate kwarg) and is mis-wired
findings.claim: PPOConfig(...) passes gradient_accumulation_steps twice, so the module raises 'SyntaxError: keyword argument repeated' at import (confirmed by python -m py_compile). Even if fixed, line 296 reads training_args.output_max_length which is never defined on the dataclass (AttributeError), and lines 316-317 call reward_model(texts) on raw strings and index output[0]['score'] as if it were a sentiment pipeline, though reward_model is an AutoModelForCausalLM.
findings.concern: UALIGN's headline method (UALIGN PPO) plus the RL-PPO and RLKF baselines all depend on this script, which cannot run as released, so the Table 1 UALIGN/RL-PPO/RLKF rows are not reproducible from the repo.
findings.resolution: Authors: please push a train_ppo.py that compiles and runs end-to-end (single gradient_accumulation_steps, a defined output_max_length, and a reward model invoked with tokenized inputs returning a scalar reward).
findings.reason: train_ppo.py:252-254 quote matches verbatim (duplicate gradient_accumulation_steps kwarg); python -m py_compile reproduces "SyntaxError: keyword argument repeated" at line 254; output_max_length (line 296) is absent from the TrainingArguments dataclass; lines 315-317 confirm reward_model(texts) is called on raw strings and indexed as output[0]["score"], inconsistent with the AutoModelForCausalLM load at line 233.

findings.title: Entropy weighting is list-replication; entropy is 0 for all known Qs
findings.claim: `list(...) * (1-conf_score)` is Python list-replication, not scalar reweighting. Because conf_score is the binary max (0 or 1), (1-conf_score) is 1 or 0: for any 'known' question (>=1 correct sample, conf_score=1) it multiplies the incorrect-answer probability list by 0, yielding [], so the entropy is identically 0 regardless of the dispersion of the sampled answers (verified in _audit_code/out/uncertainty_funcs.txt).
findings.concern: Semantic entropy — one of the two uncertainty features the paper's contribution rests on — is a constant 0 for every known question, so it carries no dispersion information there and cannot behave as Eq. 3 describes; had confidence been the paper's fractional value the line would raise TypeError.
findings.resolution: Authors: reweight the incorrect-cluster probabilities by the scalar (1-confidence) via elementwise multiplication (e.g. [p*(1-conf) for p in probs]) and confirm entropy varies across known questions.
findings.reason: uncertainty.py:50-54 quote matches verbatim; running the verbatim function (check_uncertainty_funcs.py) confirms entropy=-0.0 (identically zero) for known questions regardless of answer dispersion, and confirms list*(1-conf_score) would TypeError if confidence were fractional, only working because calculate_confidence returns int 0/1.

findings.title: Confidence is max(correctness) (binary), not the Eq. 1 mean accuracy
findings.claim: calculate_confidence is called as calculate_confidence(data['scores']['greedy_scores']) (line 98) where greedy_scores is a list of per-sample 0/1 correctness values, so it returns max = 1 if ANY sample is correct else 0 — a binary 'known' flag. The paper's Eq. 1 defines confidence as the mean (1/K)Σ 1[ŷ=y_k], a graded value; Table 4 reports a confidence distribution over the bins [0,0.25),[0.25,0.5),[0.5,0.75),[0.75,1.0].
findings.concern: The confidence feature that is embedded into the reward-model and policy prompts (uncertainty.py:149, 187) is binary, not the graded score the paper describes; this code cannot produce Table 4's multi-bin distribution, and the mean is already available as greedy_scores_avg, so the result the paper reports and the feature the method uses do not match the released code.
findings.resolution: Authors: confirm whether confidence should be greedy_scores_avg (mean, per Eq. 1); if so, correct calculate_confidence and re-derive Table 4 and the downstream features.
findings.reason: uncertainty.py:66-68 quote matches verbatim; call site at uncertainty.py:98 passes greedy_scores (binary) directly; check_uncertainty_funcs.py confirms max() returns 1 for any list with a correct sample regardless of the true mean; greedy_scores_avg exists and is used elsewhere (sample.py:306, prep.py:214, eval.py:136-147) confirming the mean was available but unused here; paper_text.txt:1765-1777 confirms the Table 4 confidence-bin distribution.

findings.title: Sampling loop produces 6 responses/question, not the paper's K=10
findings.claim: The per-question loop iterates over few_shot_examplar_list, built from generate_icl_examplar, which has 6 sets in every dataset template (triviaqa/sciq/nqopen), so exactly 6 responses are generated per question. The 10-set sample_icl_examplar loaded at line 219 is overwritten here and unused. The paper states K=10 (Sec. 3.4, Sec. 4.4).
findings.concern: The knowledge-boundary approximation uses 6 samples rather than the reported K=10, changing the confidence/entropy estimates that everything downstream depends on (and Fig. 6 explicitly reports K=10 as the chosen setting).
findings.resolution: Authors: confirm the K actually used for the released dataset, and point to the 10-exemplar set the sampling loop should iterate over.
findings.reason: sample.py:221-223 quote matches verbatim; sample.py:219 shows the unused 10-set sample_icl_examplar being overwritten at line 222/223; sample.py:252 confirms the generation loop iterates over few_shot_examplar_list; check_absence_and_counts.py confirms generate_icl_examplar has 6 sets in every dataset template while sample_icl_examplar has 10; paper_text.txt:501-502/1032/1048 confirm the paper states K=10.

findings.title: Response sampling uses greedy decoding, not temperature T=0.2
findings.quote:
# Greedy decoding by setting `do_sample=False`.
greedy_decoding_config = GenerationConfig(
    do_sample=False,
    repetition_penalty=1.0
)
findings.claim: sample.py generates every one of the K responses with hardcoded greedy decoding (do_sample=False); temperature is never applied (the temperature field defaults to 0.5 and is unused). The paper says responses are drawn with temperature T=0.2 (Sec. 2.1.1 and Sec. 3.4).
findings.concern: With greedy decoding the only source of variation across the K samples is which 1-shot prompt is randomly chosen (with replacement) — there is no temperature sampling — so the diversity that confidence and especially entropy are meant to measure differs from the paper's described procedure.
findings.resolution: Authors: confirm whether the released dataset was built greedily or at T=0.2, and if the latter, expose/enable do_sample with temperature in sample.py.
findings.reason: sample.py:266-270 quote matches verbatim; repo-wide grep of sample.py confirms only one GenerationConfig(do_sample=False) is ever built and the temperature field (line 63, default 0.5) is otherwise unreferenced; paper_text.txt:206/503/2095 confirm the paper specifies T=0.2.

findings.title: Entropy uses exact-string counting, not semantic (entailment) clustering
findings.quote:
# Count the number of occurrences of each answer
noun_counts = Counter(incorrect_ans_list)
total_nouns = sum(noun_counts.values())

# Calculate the probability of each answer
probabilities = {noun: count / total_nouns for noun, count in noun_counts.items()}
findings.claim: The 'semantic' clustering is a Counter over exact answer strings of the incorrect responses only; there is no meaning-based / bidirectional-entailment clustering. Correct answers are not clustered among themselves at all (they are collapsed into the single conf_score term). The paper defines semantic entropy via clustering semantically-equivalent responses (Eq. 2-3, citing Kuhn et al. 2023).
findings.concern: Answers that are semantically equivalent but not string-identical (e.g. 'US' vs 'United States') are treated as different clusters, and correct-answer dispersion is ignored, so the computed quantity is not the semantic entropy the paper describes.
findings.resolution: Authors: clarify whether exact-string clustering was intended; if semantic entropy per Kuhn et al. (2023) was used, add the entailment-clustering step.
findings.reason: uncertainty.py:31-36 quote matches verbatim (Counter over exact incorrect-answer strings); calculate_entropy collapses all correct answers into the single conf_score term rather than clustering them; paper_text.txt:117-276/1349 confirm the paper defines semantic entropy via Kuhn et al. (2023) semantically-equivalent-sequence clustering.
